what_its_for: This vaccine protects you against Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE), a serious brain infection caused by a virus spread through the bites of infected ticks. It is recommended if you are traveling to or living in areas of Europe or Asia where TBE is common, especially if you spend time outdoors in forests, fields, or rural areas.
how_to_take: This vaccine is given as an injection into the muscle of your upper arm by a healthcare professional (nurse or doctor). You cannot give this vaccine to yourself at home. Make sure to keep all your scheduled vaccination appointments to get full protection.
dosing: For adults and children 16 and older: You will need 3 injections total. The second shot is given 1 to 3 months after the first shot. The third shot is given 5 to 12 months after the second shot. A booster (repeat) dose is recommended every 3 years if you remain at risk. For children aged 1 to 15 years: The schedule is the same, but a child-strength dose is used. A faster schedule is also available if you need protection more quickly before travel — talk to your doctor about this option.
missed_dose: If you miss or are late for a scheduled dose, contact your doctor or pharmacist as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to skip any doses, as all 3 shots are needed for full protection. You do not need to restart the series if you are late — you can usually continue from where you left off.
storage: This vaccine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. It must be kept refrigerated at 2°C to 8°C (36°F to 46°F). It should never be frozen. Keep it away from direct light. Do not use the vaccine if it has been frozen, looks cloudy, or contains visible particles.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting this vaccine if you currently have a moderate to severe illness with a fever — wait until you have recovered. Do not get this vaccine if you have had a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose of TBE vaccine or to any of its ingredients, including components derived from eggs or chicken protein. Tell your doctor about all allergies before vaccination.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek medical help right away if you experience: difficulty breathing or swallowing, swelling of your face, lips, or throat, rapid heartbeat, dizziness or feeling faint, a high fever (above 39°C / 102°F), seizures, or any other severe reaction after getting the shot. Mild side effects such as soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site, headache, tiredness, or a low-grade fever are common and usually go away on their own within a day or two. Call your doctor if these do not improve or get worse.
when_it_works: You are not fully protected until you have received all 3 doses of the vaccine. Some protection begins after the first 2 doses, but the best and longest-lasting protection comes after completing the full 3-dose series. Try to start your vaccination series well in advance of travel — ideally several months before you leave.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: There is limited data on the safety of TBE vaccine during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor to weigh the risks and benefits before getting vaccinated. Children under 1 year: This vaccine is not approved for use in babies younger than 1 year of age. Elderly patients (over 60): The vaccine can be used, but older adults may have a slightly lower immune response. Your doctor may monitor you more closely. Immunocompromised patients: If your immune system is weakened due to illness or medications, the vaccine may be less effective. Talk to your doctor about the best approach for you.
